title: Create and update columns
goal: Calculate new fields, tidy column names, and change selected values safely.
prerequisites: Know arithmetic, column selection, Boolean masks, and assignment.

cells.title: Calculate a new column
cells.explanation: Assign a Series to a new column name to add a field. Arithmetic across columns works row by row after index alignment. Here the artificial Score_Per_Hour ratio demonstrates division; it is not a validated measure of student ability. Always consider units and the meaning of a calculation.
cells.code:
df = students()
df["Score_Per_Hour"] = df["Score"] / df["Study_Hours"]
result = df[["Name", "Score", "Study_Hours", "Score_Per_Hour"]]
print(result.head(3).round(2))

questions.prompt: Which part of the assignment names the new column?
What is Amira's Score_Per_Hour before rounding?
Why should a high ratio not be treated as proof of better learning?
questions.answer: The ratio alone does not measure learning quality or account for other factors. It is only an arithmetic example with fictional data.

cells.task: Start with a fresh df = students(). Create Score_Fraction by dividing Score by 100. Store Name, Score, and Score_Fraction for all students in result, then print its first three rows.
cells.hint: Assign the division result to df["Score_Fraction"].
cells.solution:
df = students()
df["Score_Fraction"] = df["Score"] / 100
result = df[["Name", "Score", "Score_Fraction"]]
print(result.head(3))
cells.solution_note: The first fractions are 0.88, 0.72, and 0.91. The original Score remains measured out of 100.

check.prompt: What happens when you assign to a column name that does not yet exist?
check.feedback: Assigning a value or aligned Series to a new name creates a column.

cells.verify:
assert df.shape == (12, 10) and result.loc[0, 'Score_Per_Hour'] == 11
assert round(result.loc[1, 'Score_Per_Hour'], 1) == 14.4
cells.watch: Before dividing by a column, check for zero and missing denominators; they can create undefined results.
cells.takeaway: I can create a calculated column and state its units and limits.

cells.title: Use assign, rename, and drop
cells.explanation: assign() returns a DataFrame with new or replaced columns. rename(columns=...) changes column labels, while drop(columns=...) removes named columns. These methods return new objects by default. Assign the returned result so your intended changes are kept.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = (df.assign(Passed=df["Score"] >= 60)
            .rename(columns={"Name": "Student_Name"})
            .drop(columns=["Join_Date"]))
print(result[["Student_Name", "Score", "Passed"]].head(4))
print("Result shape:", result.shape)

questions.prompt: What is stored in the new Passed column?
questions.answer: True for scores at least 60 and False otherwise, using the rule stated in this example.

questions.prompt: Does result still have a column named Name?
questions.answer: No. In result it has been renamed Student_Name. The original df still has Name.

questions.prompt: Why does the final table still have nine columns?
questions.answer: It starts with nine, adds Passed, then drops Join_Date: 9 + 1 - 1 = 9.

cells.task: Use assign to create Needs_Support for scores below 70. Rename Attendance to Attendance_Percent and drop Join_Date. Keep the result in result.
cells.hint: Provide a Boolean Series to assign, a mapping to rename, and a list of names to drop.
cells.solution_note: Needs_Support is True for Dana, Hassan, and Khalid. The longer attendance name makes the unit explicit. df remains available in its original form.

check.prompt: Which removes a named column from the returned table?
check.feedback: drop(columns=[...]) removes the specified columns; rename changes a label and assign creates or replaces values.

cells.verify:
assert result.shape == (12, 9) and 'Name' not in result and 'Student_Name' in result
assert 'Join_Date' not in result and result['Passed'].sum() == 11
assert 'Name' in df and 'Passed' not in df
cells.solution_verify:
assert result['Needs_Support'].sum() == 3 and 'Attendance_Percent' in result
assert 'Attendance' not in result and 'Join_Date' not in result
assert 'Attendance' in df and 'Needs_Support' not in df
cells.watch: Calling df.drop(...) without assigning its returned result does not change df by default.
cells.takeaway: I can add fields and tidy column structure while keeping the original available.

cells.title: Update the original with one loc assignment
cells.explanation: Use one .loc[row_condition, column_name] assignment to change selected values in a DataFrame. This explicitly identifies both the rows and the field being changed. Avoid chained assignment such as df[mask]["Score"] = value; it does not reliably update the intended original object and does not do so under pandas 3 Copy-on-Write.
cells.code:
df = students()
mask = df["Student_ID"] == "S004"
df.loc[mask, "Score"] = 67
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)

questions.prompt: Which row and column are changed?
questions.answer: The Score column for the row whose Student_ID is S004, Dana.

questions.prompt: What is Dana's score after the assignment?
Why does a single loc assignment state your intention more clearly than two chained brackets?
questions.answer: It tells pandas to change the named column in selected rows of df itself, instead of writing into an intermediate selection.

cells.task: Apply a practice bonus of 3 points to students with Attendance at least 95. Cap scores at 100 and show only the updated students.
cells.hint: Use one .loc[mask, "Score"] assignment; calculate from the same selected Score values and clip at 100.
cells.solution:
df = students()
mask = df["Attendance"] >= 95
df.loc[mask, "Score"] = (df.loc[mask, "Score"] + 3).clip(upper=100)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score", "Attendance"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Amira, Chloe, Fatima, and Jamal receive the practice bonus. Their scores become 91, 94, 98, and 92. Students outside the mask keep their scores.

check.prompt: Which is the clear way to update selected scores in df?
check.feedback: One loc assignment directly targets the selected rows and column in df.

cells.solution_verify:
assert result['Student_ID'].tolist() == ['S001', 'S003', 'S006', 'S010']
assert result['Score'].tolist() == [91, 94, 98, 92]
assert df.loc[df['Student_ID'] == 'S004', 'Score'].iloc[0] == 65
cells.watch: Repeatedly running an incremental update on the same table would repeat the bonus; this cell starts with a fresh table each time.
cells.takeaway: I can modify selected values using one explicit loc assignment.

cells.title: Keep an independent working copy
cells.explanation: Assigning original to another name creates an alias: both names refer to the same Python object. copy() creates a separate DataFrame for this ordinary scalar-valued teaching table. Use a fresh copy when you want to experiment without changing the original. Pandas copy rules do not replace the need to understand which object you are editing.
cells.code:
original = students()
working = original.copy()
working.loc[0, "Score"] = 0
print("Original first score:", original.loc[0, "Score"])
print("Working first score:", working.loc[0, "Score"])
print("Same object:", working is original)

questions.prompt: What does .copy() let us do in this example?
questions.answer: Change values in working while keeping original unchanged.

questions.prompt: What two first-score values are printed?
What would change if the code used working = original instead?
questions.answer: Both names would refer to the same object; changing working would also be visible through original.

cells.task: Copy only the RAK rows into working. Add 1 to their scores in the copy and verify Amira's original score is still 88.
cells.hint: Filter with loc, call .copy(), and update the selected table rather than original.
cells.solution:
original = students()
working = original.loc[original["Campus"] == "RAK"].copy()
working["Score"] = working["Score"] + 1
print(working[["Name", "Score"]])
print("Amira in original:", original.loc[0, "Score"])
cells.solution_note: working contains six RAK students with scores increased by 1. Amira has 89 in working and 88 in original.

options: Makes two names refer to the same object.
Always creates a separate deep copy.
Exports the data to a file.
check.feedback: Simple assignment binds another name to the existing object; copy() is a separate operation.

cells.verify:
assert original.loc[0, 'Score'] == 88 and working.loc[0, 'Score'] == 0
assert working is not original
cells.solution_verify:
assert len(working) == 6 and working.loc[0, 'Score'] == 89
assert original.loc[0, 'Score'] == 88 and original.shape == (12, 9)
cells.watch: For columns containing nested mutable Python objects, even a deep DataFrame copy does not recursively copy those inner objects; this table uses ordinary scalar values.
cells.takeaway: I can protect source values while testing changes on a separate table.
